analysis.subject: civics
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers the campaign for the 19th amendment from its introduction in Congress in 1878 through state suffrage laws by 1912, support shifts in 1917 and 1918, congressional passage on May 21, 1919, Tennessee ratification on August 18, 1920, certification on August 26, 1920, and ongoing limits on voting rights afterward.

overview.headline: Struggle for womens voting rights and constitutional ratification

keyPoints.point: The 19th amendment legally guarantees American women the right to vote after decades of struggle.
keyPoints.quote: The 19th amendment legally guarantees American women the right to vote.

keyPoints.point: Suffragists pursued a strategy of passing suffrage acts in western states before a federal amendment succeeded.
keyPoints.quote: Some pursued a strategy of passing suffrage acts in each state—nine western states adopted woman suffrage legislation by 1912.

keyPoints.point: Political balance began to shift after New York adopted woman suffrage in 1917 and President Wilson changed to support an amendment in 1918.
keyPoints.quote: When New York adopted woman suffrage in 1917 and President Wilson changed his position to support an amendment in 1918, the political balance began to shift.

keyPoints.point: The amendment met its final hurdle when Tennessee became the 36th state and the agreement of three-fourths of the states was obtained.
keyPoints.quote: the amendment passed its final hurdle of obtaining the agreement of three-fourths of the states

keyPoints.point: Many women remained unable to vote long into the 20th century because discriminatory state laws continued to limit voting.
keyPoints.quote: Many women remained unable to vote long into the 20th century because of discriminatory state voting laws.

keyTerms.gloss: Right to vote sought through state legislation and western campaigns
keyTerms.quote: nine western states adopted woman suffrage legislation by 1912

keyTerms.gloss: Formal constitutional change to guarantee voting rights
keyTerms.quote: By 1916, almost all of the major suffrage organizations were united behind the goal of a constitutional amendment.

keyTerms.gloss: Certified approval by states after required agreement
keyTerms.quote: Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the ratification on August 26, 1920

keyTerms.gloss: Full voting rights that ratification alone did not ensure
keyTerms.quote: yet ratification did not ensure full enfranchisement

keyTerms.gloss: Nonviolent protest to achieve radical change in law
keyTerms.quote: practiced civil disobedience to achieve what many Americans considered a radical change of the Constitution

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Helps learners order the amendment process from congressional passage to state ratification and certification as taught on the page.
componentPlan.focusQuote: On May 21, 1919, the House of Representatives passed the amendment, and 2 weeks later, the Senate followed.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Checks recall of strategies, political shifts, ratification requirement, and continued limits on voting rights.
componentPlan.focusQuote: Many women remained unable to vote long into the 20th century because of discriminatory state voting laws.
